lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- The Meeting That Ends On Time
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Tiago (Mock Rodízio) | Lesson 5 -- The Meeting That Ends On Time

listenings.text: Tiago, it's Michael. I just came out of the call with your plant manager and I want to be straight with you. Fifty minutes. We talked about the press, we talked about the audit, we talked about somebody's holiday in October, and I put the phone down without knowing one single thing that is going to happen next. Nobody said who does what. Nobody said by when. The delay is fine, I can plan around a delay. What I cannot plan around is not knowing. Next time, you run it. Ten minutes, three things, and tell me who owns each one.

gist.prompt: Listen to the voicemail. What is Michael's complaint?
choices: The delay itself — he cannot accept it.
The meeting ended without decisions, owners or dates.
He was not invited to the meeting.

items: The press, the audit, and somebody's holiday in October.
Michael says the delay is unacceptable.
"The delay is fine, I can plan around a delay."
Someone was given a clear task in the meeting.
"Nobody said who does what. Nobody said by when."
Michael wants the next meeting to be longer and more detailed.
He asks Tiago to run the next one.

post_skill.title: What do you think?
items: Michael says he can plan around a delay but not around not knowing. Is that true in your job too?
Fifty minutes and three subjects. What would you have cut?
Is it easier to run a meeting or to sit in one? Why?
Whose job was it to close that meeting — honestly?
What would change at your work if every meeting ended with owners and dates?

language.label: Target language — what the person running the meeting says
items: We have ten minutes — let's take the first item.
Let's put a date on that.
So the action is yours, by Friday.
We're at time — let's stop there.

language.title: Six of them do six different jobs. Match each line to its job.
defs: turns an intention into something you can check later
moves a real subject out of this meeting without killing it
ends on time, which is what makes people come next time
makes sure everyone leaves with the same version
gives the task a name, not a department

language.text: Look at how short the interruption is: "Can I stop you there?" — five words, no apology. In Portuguese we soften an interruption with a long sentence, and in English that long sentence costs you the turn: by the time you finish it, the other person is speaking again. The politeness lives in the question mark, not in the length.

pre_comm.title: Someone in the meeting says this. Answer as the person running it, using the expression given — then say the whole line out loud.
items: "So, are we all here? What are we talking about today?"
"...and that reminds me of the problem we had in 2023 with the other supplier, which started when..."
"While we're here, can we talk about the invoices?"

pre_comm.title: Reveal answer key
list: We have ten minutes — let's take the first item.
Can I stop you there? Let's come back to the press.
Let's park that for now — I'll put it on Thursday's list.
Who owns this? I need a name, not a department.
Let's put a date on that. Friday?
To recap: three things. The press, the audit, and October.
pre_comm.note: Accept justified variations. After each one, say it out loud: which sounds more natural in your voice?

items: You are running the call Michael asked for: ten minutes, three items. Your teacher is Denise, the only other person on it.
The agenda — three items, in your order
(1) The press: maintenance comes Friday, and the October slot is tight. (2) The audit in March: one supplier still has no certificate. (3) October holidays: two operators are away the same week.
Open it, keep it to ten minutes, and finish with THREE outcomes: each item either has an owner and a date, or is parked. Denise will not help you do that.

task1.label: Useful language
items: We have ten minutes — let's take the first item.
Let's put a date on that.

The call is over. Michael was not on it, and he is the one who asked for it. Record the summary you would send him as a voice message: what was decided, who owns each item, by when, and what was parked.
Ninety seconds maximum. Three items, three outcomes — an owner and a date, or the word parked. Nothing else.

task2.title: Before you record
items: In what order will you say the three items — the order they happened, or the order that matters to Michael?
Which item has the weakest outcome? Say that one honestly instead of dressing it up.
What is your first sentence? Say it out loud before you start recording.

task2.text: Now record it. Your teacher only holds the clock — no help, no interruptions.

feedback.title: Focus on accuracy
items: When Denise went off-topic, how long did it take you to stop her? What did you say?
Which of the three items ended without an owner or a date — and why that one?
Say one sentence you got stuck on. Say it again now, the way you wanted it.
Five lessons: reporting, asking, recommending, warning, running the meeting. Which one have you already used for real at work?
